profile.summary: 1 Chronicles is a historical re-reading focused on rekindling hope among the Jews of the post-exile. Instead of just recording the past, the book organizes the memory of Israel to show that the small community of Judah, rebuilding itself amidst the opposition, remained tied to God's promises. The narrative begins with genealogies that connect the people from Adam to the returnees of exile and then concentrates on Saul, David, and preparation for the temple. The theological center of the book is in the promise made to David: the kingdom of God would follow by its lineage, and the restored community in Jerusalem should live as a sign of that hope. The emphasis lies less in political power and more in identity, fidelity to the covenant, worship and continuity of divine purpose.
profile.setting: The backdrop is the period after the fall of Judah before the Babylonians, between 605 and 586 BC, followed by the Persian ascension under Cyrus, which allowed the return of exiles to Judah after the fall of Babylon in 539 BC. The community that returned to Jerusalem was small, vulnerable and without real political autonomy. She faced hostility, contempt and social pressure while trying to rebuild the temple and preserve its faith and identity. The book was probably composed around 400 BC in or near Jerusalem in late Persian times. Authorship is traditionally attributed to Ezra, but this is not demonstrable; the author, called Chronost here, remains anonymous. The date and context suggest an environment in which the central question was how God's people could exist faithfully under imperial rule.

structure.label: Genealogy and identity of Israel
structure.description: He presents the lineage from Adam to the returnees of exile, highlighting the continuity of the people and their tribes, with special attention to Judah, Levi, and Benjamin.

structure.label: Saul and the Ascension of David
structure.description: It shows Saul's fall for his infidelity and the consolidation of David as king, with increasing support from Israel.

structure.label: The Ark in Jerusalem
structure.description: He describes the transfer of the ark to Jerusalem, a decisive event for the affirmation of the kingdom of David.

structure.label: The promise to David and the Expansion of the Kingdom
structure.description: He exposes the divine promise about the dynasty of David and the political unfoldings that paved the way for the future construction of the temple.

structure.label: Preparation of the temple and organization of the kingdom
structure.description: Gather the necessary elements for the temple, including the site, materials, plans, and organization of officers and Levites.

structure.label: Assembly and commissioning of Solomon
structure.description: Closure with the public convocation, the surrender of the temple plans and the presentation of Solomon as the king of peace that will build him.

themes: Fidelity to the covenant in times of frailty
Identity of God's people after exile
Centrality of the temple, worship and the Levites
The Davidic Promise as a Source of Hope
Infidelity as the root of judgment and ruin
readingKeys: Notice how genealogies are not mere list: they affirm continuity, belonging, and historical purpose.
Compare Saul and David as two opposing models of response to God: one marked by infidelity, the other by the preparation of the kingdom and the worship.
Note that the focus of the book is not on political independence, but in the hope of restoration linked to the promise made to David and to the life of fidelity before God.
profile.cautions: The book was written for a specific post-exile audience and selects the past in a theological way, not as a neutral or complete history. Authorship is traditionally linked to Ezra, but this identification is uncertain. The date is also approximate, probably located at the end of the Persian period, around 400 BC. It is important to read 1 Chronicles as a work that interprets history to strengthen the identity and hope of the community, not as a simple repetition of previous books.

dossier.narratedEra: The narrative of 1 Chronicles takes place from Adam and the patriarchs, passes through the formation of Israel, through the period of the united monarchy, especially Saul and David, and culminates in the preparation of Solomon's temple and coronation. The notes emphasize that the work looks to Israel's past to interpret it in the light of the identity of the restored people in Judah after exile.
dossier.compositionEra: The work was composed, according to the notes, at the end of the Persian Empire, probably around 400 BC, in or near Jerusalem. Tyndale's introduction highlights the traditional proposal of Ezra, but notes that the author does not explicitly identify; the date is inferred by internal references, the genealogy of Jeconia and the absence of Greek linguistic or ideological traits. Matthew Henry also associates the work with Ezra, but treats this as a traditional assumption.

politics.title: Judah as Persian province, not sovereign kingdom
politics.detail: The introduction describes the community of Judah after exile as a small province within the vast Persian Empire, without real political autonomy. The focus of the chronicler, then, is not to narrate national independence, but to support the vocation of God's people in condition of imperial subordination.
politics.readingImpact: This prevents reading 1 Chronicles as propaganda of immediate political restoration; the book consoles a powerless community, reaffirming its importance in the divine plan.

politics.title: Babylon, fall to Cyrus and Authorized Return
politics.detail: The notes place the fall of Babylon in 539 BC and say that Cyrus, by expanding his empire, allowed the return of the Jewish exiles to Judea and the organization of a province around Jerusalem. The context includes physical protection and some economic independence, but not sovereignty.
politics.readingImpact: The reading of 1 Chronicles gains the tone of a community in partial restoration: there is a return and percultual reordering, but under foreign hegemony.

politics.title: Saul, David and the succession of the monarchy
politics.detail: Tyndale summarizes the transition from royalty: Saul dies out of infidelity and David takes over the throne afterwards. The work explains Saul's fall as an initial example of the dynamics of infidelity marking other kings of Judah.
politics.readingImpact: The monarchy is read theologically, not only politically: legitimacy depends on fidelity to God, and Saul's failure prepares David's centrality.

politics.title: Political conditions for the temple under David
politics.detail: In the chapters of David, the introduction says that he prepares the political conditions necessary for the temple: organization of officers, control of the space of worship, and consolidation of Jerusalem as the center of the kingdom. The transfer of the ark is described as a key event for the structuring of the Davidic realm.
politics.readingImpact: The temple appears as a project that requires political and liturgical order; Jerusalem is not only capital, but the center of the divine presence and national-religious identity.

politics.title: Persians, local leadership and relative date of composition
politics.detail: The date of around 400 BC. it is defended because the genealogy of the descendants of Jeconiah suggests a distance of about eight generations from Zerubbabel, linked to the period of Darius. The note also mentions that the work is probably after Nehemiah's departure to Jerusalem in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes.
politics.readingImpact: The book is best read as a reflection of a community already installed in the Persian order, and not as text of the monarchical period or the beginning of the return.

customs.title: Genealogy as preservation of identity and territory
customs.detail: The introduction explains that genealogies answer two central questions: who the story is and where these people live. They preserve the connection with the past and identity of a community without political influence.
customs.readingImpact: The lists are not just appendix; they help the reader to see belonging, continuity and historical location as part of the people's faith.

customs.title: Centrality of the temple and the Levites
customs.detail: Tyndale highlights the chronicler's strong interest in the temple, his services and, in particular, the Levites. In 15:1-3, the Levites are called to carry the ark because this was their responsibility, and in 15:16-22 lists of Levitical musicians with distinct functions appear.
customs.readingImpact: The cult is presented as an organized community structure; fidelity includes specific functions, order and service designated.

customs.title: Ark in special tent, not in the tabernacle of Gibeon
customs.detail: The note informs that David prepared a special tent for the ark in Jerusalem, but that this was not the tabernacle, which was in Gibeon at that time.
customs.readingImpact: The reader perceives the coexistence of cult centers and the ritual transition in progress; Jerusalem becomes the unique place of the ark without immediately abolishing the rest of the cult structure.

customs.title: Volunteer offer for the temple
customs.detail: In 29:1-9, the leaders of Israel offer gifts to the Lord in a voluntary manner, in parallel with the generous disposition seen in the preparation of the tabernacle. The note points out that the financial weight of the temple did not fall only on Solomon, as David and the leaders had already contributed.
customs.readingImpact: The construction of the temple is read as a community and cult enterprise, supported by voluntary generosity, not only by real imposition.

customs.title: Sacrifices, anointing and coronation together
customs.detail: At the close of David's reign, sacrifices accompany speeches and prayers, then come the anointing of Solomon and Zadok, and then enthronement. The note about Zadok clarifies that he is not initiating his priesthood, but being dedicated to the service of the temple.
customs.readingImpact: Coronation is not just political; it is liturgical and priestly. The real power is surrounded by worship and consecration.

language.title: "The events of the days" and "anais"
language.detail: The introduction of Matthew Henry explains that the Hebrew title refers to the events of the days, i.e. records or annals. Jerome, in the Latin tradition, calls the work of chronikon, a record of ancient events. The Septuagint calls it "the things left," as a complement to Kings.
language.readingImpact: The form of the book is historical and selective: it does not attempt to replace other accounts, but to organize records to teach and remember.

language.title: Repeat as a pedagogical resource, no empty redundancy
language.detail: Matthew Henry insists that repetition of sacred things is useful; Chronicles repeats previous material to establish testimony, memory, and security. He compares it, in principle, to the repetition found in the gospels.
language.readingImpact: The reader must wait parallel and resumed as a theological and pastoral strategy, and not as a simple copy without purpose.

language.title: Genealogy as an answer to two historical questions
language.detail: Tyndale says that the chronicler entered genealogies to answer who needed to have his story told and where this people lived. The list of descents shows divine selection from Adam to Jacob and then to the post-exile.
language.readingImpact: The lists gain identity and territorial function: the text builds belonging amid dispersion and fragility.

language.title: "Unit of Israel" despite the division
language.detail: The introduction holds that the chronicler sees all the tribes as present in the restoration, including those of the north. Thus, Israel is understood as a people of faith, not as a sovereign political entity.
language.readingImpact: The language of Israel in 1 Chronicles must be read in theological key: tribal unity and common inheritance remain relevant even after the end of the divided kingdom.

language.title: Titles and musical lists with technical specifications
language.detail: In 15:20-21, the notes clarify musical terms preserved in Hebrew: "Alamoth" probably indicates an acute record, and "Sheminith" may suggest octave or more serious record. The note shows that the text preserves specific musical instructions.
language.readingImpact: The liturgical scene becomes more concrete: the cult involves technical organization and musical specialization, not only devotional improvisation.

language.title: Darics as equivalent of monetary update
language.detail: On 29:7, Tyndale notes that the 10,000 gold coins correspond to Persian darics, minted in the reign of Darius I, and that the chronicler would have converted the values to the equivalents of his own time.
language.readingImpact: The reader understands that the amount is transmitted in comprehensible monetary language to the later public, without requiring literalistic reading of the old pesos.

timeline.title: Fall of Judah before Babylon
timeline.detail: The introduction places the Babylonian conquest of Judah between 605 and 586 BC as a previous history of exile.
timeline.readingImpact: 1 Chronicles are born to a community marked by national trauma and loss of wealth, which explains their tone of hope and memory.

timeline.title: Fall of Babylon and Persian ascension
timeline.detail: In 539 BC, Babylon falls without resistance, and Cyrus' empire stretches westward, incorporating Babylon.
timeline.readingImpact: The imperial change explains why the Jewish return becomes possible and why the book speaks to a Persian, non- Babylonian context.

timeline.title: Return and reconstruction under difficulties
timeline.detail: The period of return is marked by spiritual restoration, physical protection and limited economic independence, but also by mockery and opposition of neighboring peoples in rebuilding the temple and after the wall.
timeline.readingImpact: The 1 Chronicle narrative responds to a community that already experiences incomplete restoration and external pressure.

timeline.title: Zorobabel and the Backdrop of Darius
timeline.detail: The note mentions Zorobabel as governor around 520 BC, in the days of Darius, to support the approximate chronology of the composition.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader realizes that the work looks to a recent post-exile past, but writes a few generations after these first returned.

timeline.title: Nehemiah in 445 BC as a later milestone
timeline.detail: Tyndale assumes that 1 Chronicles were written after Nehemiah's departure to Jerusalem in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes in 445 BC, when he repaired the city walls.
timeline.readingImpact: This data situates the work after important reforms of the post-exile, reinforcing its vocation to reinterpret the identity of Judah already restored.

timeline.title: Probable period of composition about 400 BC.
timeline.detail: The notes conclude that the work was written in the final part of the Persian period, around 400 BC, and not in the Greek period, as there is no linguistic or ideological evidence of Hellenistic influence.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader should place the book in a late Persian moment, in which the Jewish community seeks stability and meaning, not in an already Hellenized age.

investigation: The coverage of the sources is strongly concentrated on the introductions and three blocks of chapters (1, 15 and 29); therefore, several central themes of the book do not appear here because they were not discussed in the attached notes.
The traditional attribution to Ezra is mentioned, but treated as tradition, not as proven data; Matthew Henry's note also takes it conjecturally.

The date of composition around 400 BC. is an inference of the notes, not an absolute date; the material itself recognizes that it is a approximation based on genealogy, Persian context and absence of greek marks.
The political and social categories were filled only when the notes explain them or allow controlled inference; no independent historical reconstructions were added.
Some language elements are technical and restricted, such as musical terms and the title of the book; there is no broad treatment of style, vocabulary or Hebrewism in the sources.

The customs section was limited to worship, levistic organization, provision of resources and coronation because the attached notes do not develop details of food, clothing or daily economy beyond the context of the temple.

Reading is consciously confessional and evangelical, but here the limit requested was preserved: the statements were taken only as what the secondary sources say, always distinguishing between explicit source, interpretation and debated points.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends solely on the introductions of Tyndale and Matthew Henry and the notes of 1 Chronicles 1, 15 and 29. Thus, he offers a substantial, yet selective view of the book. The sources do not cover in equal detail all chapters, nor do they systematically discuss archaeology, external chronology, textual criticism or broad academic debates about authorship and composition. They also do not provide enough data for a complete reconstruction of Judah's daily life in the post-exile; therefore, customs such as food, clothing, housing and common work appear only indirectly or do not appear. In addition, several statements about the context are presented by the notes as historical or literary inferences, and not as independent evidence. Where the source only suggests, the label was maintained as interpretation; where there is debate or uncertainty, this was preserved rather than harmonized.
